before the first <note>process</note> (in the stomach), which is called <term>chylificatio</term> <gloss>chylification/conversion of food into chyle</gloss>. The excrements of the first and second <term>coctio</term> <gloss>digestion/cooking</gloss> (namely in the intestines, and in the gall bladder and urinary bladder) are contemporaneous with the organs that cook them. Finally, not only in the vegetative part of the soul, but even before the soul itself, there exists a mind, providence, and intellect; which immediately, from the very beginning, arrange, order, and provide for everything toward the being and well-being of the chick; and which fashion, with art, the form and likeness of the generators.

Regarding the likeness of the offspring, it is permitted to doubt what the cause might be why sometimes the fetus is found to be more like the father, sometimes the mother, and sometimes even like ancestors, whether paternal or maternal; especially when, in a single union and at the same moment, several eggs are fertilized. It is also admirable that virtues and vices, diseases as well as scars and birthmarks, are transferred from the progenitors to the descendants; and this happens in only some fetuses, not in all. In the poultry genus, some are high-spirited and born for battle, preferring to die rather than yield to adversaries by fleeing: yet their descendants, unless they have been born from similar parents, gradually shed that virtue; according to the saying: the brave are created from the brave. In many other species of animals as well (and especially in humans), the nobility of the breed is observed; and many gifts of mind and body arrive through <term>tradux</term> <gloss>transmission/derivation</gloss>.

I have often wondered why, since we see that offspring usually obtain a certain mixed structure or composition from both parents, and this in all other parts, the same does not occur in the genitals; but generally either a male or a female is born, and very rarely a hermaphrodite.

Finally, many things exist before they appear; and some are begun among the first things, which are completed last; such as the eyes, the genitals, and the beak.

Doubts and certain difficulties also arise from this regarding the primacy of the members or the dignity of the parts.

<summary>Harvey examines the mysterious inheritance of parental traits and the rarity of hermaphroditism, while noting that fetal organs develop in a specific sequence.</summary>
